draft.title: Skewed, symmetric and bimodal shapes
card: Symmetric
the data is balanced, so the left side of the display mirrors the right. Most values sit in the middle and fewer sit at both ends.
Skewed
the data has one long tail. If the tail stretches to the right (high values), it is positively skewed. If it stretches to the left (low values), it is negatively skewed.
Bimodal
the data has two clear peaks, with a dip between them. It often means two different groups are mixed together.

Look at where the bars are tallest and where the tail goes. Example: most students in a class have 0 to 2 pets and a few have 8 or more. The tail points to the high values, so the data is positively skewed.

4.alt: A histogram of pets per student in classes of width 2. The counts are 10, 8, 4, 2 and 1, so the tallest bar is on the left and a tail stretches to the right.

draft.remember: Symmetric is balanced, skewed has one long tail, and bimodal has two peaks.

a.q: A histogram has its tallest bars on the right and a long tail stretching to the left. How is the data described?
a.why: The tail points to the low values on the left, so the data is negatively skewed. It is not positively skewed, because the skew is named by the side of the tail, not by where the tall bars are.
a.clue: Name the shape by the direction of the tail.

b.q: A shop records the ages of its customers. Many are about 15 to 20 and many are about 60 to 65, with few in between. What is the shape of the data?
opts: Bimodal, as there are two peaks
Positively skewed, as it has old customers
Negatively skewed, as it has young customers
b.why: There are two separate peaks with a dip between them, so the data is bimodal. It may look balanced, but a symmetric shape has one centre of tall bars, not two peaks.

b.best: Bimodal, as there are two peaks

problems.detail: The example says most students have 0 to 2 pets, but the histogram shows only 10 of 25 students in the 0–2 class (40%), so the chart does not show 'most'.
The symmetric line says most values sit in the middle with fewer at both ends. Symmetric data need not be like this: a uniform or two-peaked balanced shape is also symmetric.
The why says a symmetric shape has one centre of tall bars, not two peaks. Bimodal data can also be symmetric, so the two shapes are not mutually exclusive. Bimodal is still the best answer here.

proposal.title: Skewed, symmetric and bimodal shapes
card: Symmetric
the data is balanced, so the left half of the display roughly mirrors the right half. Often the tallest bars are in the middle, with shorter bars at both ends.
Skewed
the data has one long tail. If the tail stretches to the right (high values), it is positively skewed. If it stretches to the left (low values), it is negatively skewed.
Bimodal
the data has two clear peaks, with a dip between them. It often means two different groups are mixed together.

Look at where the bars are tallest and where the tail goes. Example: in a class, the tallest bar is for 0 to 1 pets, and the bars shrink towards 8 to 9 pets. The tail points to the high values, so the data is positively skewed.
